name: Maya Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Maya, thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Pennant Office Supply in Ashby, ordering paper, toner, pens and folders from about forty suppliers. I start at eight, go through the low-stock list, and ring or email the suppliers. I check each delivery's invoice against what we ordered. Mr Okafor, the owner, signs off the big ones. I've been here four years and I still ask Ivo, the young guy, when the system acts up.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks. What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like it when everything arrives on time and nobody calls me to complain. I don't like the numbers, because sales go down every year. At home it's Marcos, who drives a bread van, and our kids, Beatriz and Tiago. We get through, but there's never a spare week of money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I knew it, those people on the news always overdo it. At work, nothing, I'd keep ordering as usual. At home Marcos would say see, and we'd move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Private view: it doesn't fix my problem. Pennant sells paper and pens to offices, and offices buy less every year because everything's on screens. So even without AI I'm worried the firm shrinks and I'm the one who was hired last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, order from the same suppliers, ring the same people, check my paper lists. I'd ask my sister, who runs a hair salon, if I could do her books and ordering on Saturdays for extra money. And I'd put off the new kitchen again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight, like always. It's not panic, it's a low hum, the kind where you're counting at the supermarket till.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said offices buy less every year. How do you see that at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Toner and copy paper are down about a fifth since I started four years ago. Mr Okafor keeps saying it'll bounce back. I don't see it bouncing, I see more empty shelves in the warehouse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you mean about putting off the kitchen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our kitchen has had a broken cupboard door for two years. We keep saying we'll fix the cupboard door when there's money, and there's never money. It's a small thing, but it tells you how the budget is.

say: I'd say I knew it: the people on the news always **overdo** it.
At work I'd change nothing and keep **ordering** as usual.
think: It doesn't fix my problem: offices buy **less** paper every year.
The firm may shrink even without AI, and I was hired **last**.
do: Keep ordering from the same **suppliers** and ringing the same people.
Ask my sister, who runs a hair salon, for Saturday **bookkeeping** work.
feel: A low **hum** of tightness, like counting at the supermarket till.
S0.quote: We keep saying we'll fix the cupboard door when there's money, and there's never money.
fieldNote: Her anxiety comes from a **shrinking** firm, not from AI; hype changes little for her.
Keeps to **routine** and small fixes such as Saturday work for her sister.
Uses everyday **household** details, such as the broken cupboard, to show how tight money is.

steps.text: Keep ordering from the same suppliers and checking the paper lists
Do the hair salon's ordering and books on Saturdays for pay
Put off the new kitchen again

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nothing at work, honestly. Mr Okafor's the type to let people go quietly. To my friends I'd say it's going to be hard for people like me, and the government should look at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The card says buying. That's me. Most of what I do is look at a list and reorder, then check the invoice matches. A program does that in a second. With Pennant already shrinking, the owner will say we can't afford three buyers, and I'm the newest and the one who never learned the computer stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get ahead of the layoff by learning one thing, the new ordering system, if Pennant buys one. Marcos would help me practise at the kitchen table. I'd also go to the job centre and look at roles that deal with people, like a customer desk at the council. And I'd ask my mum to take the kids two afternoons a week so I can take extra shifts anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. I'd feel it on my chest as soon as I wake up. I keep imagining the day Mr Okafor calls me into the small office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never learned the computer stuff. What holds you back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not good at it, and I hate feeling stupid in front of the younger ones. When Ivo shows me a shortcut I nod and forget it. I know it's a bad habit, and if my job depended on it I'd have to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you and Marcos cover the bills if you lost your pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marcos drives a bread van, so his wage covers the mortgage but nothing else. We'd cut the phones to the cheapest plan, no more holidays, and my mum would feed the kids some nights. A few weeks, then we'd have to pick which card to pay.

say: I'd say nothing at work; the owner lets people go **quietly**.
I'd tell friends it will be hard for people like me, and the **government** should look at it.
think: Buying is me: I look at a list, reorder, and check the **invoice**.
With the firm already shrinking, the owner won't keep three buyers, and I'm **newest**.
I never learned the computer side, which is my **weak spot**.
do: Learn the new ordering **system** if Pennant buys one, practising with my partner at the kitchen table.
Go to the job centre and look at **customer desk** roles.
Ask my mum to take the kids two **afternoons** so I can take extra shifts.
feel: **Heavy** on my chest from the moment I wake up.
S1.quote: I hate feeling stupid in front of the younger ones.
fieldNote: Fear of the **small office** call dominates; she expects to be cut as the newest and least tech-confident.
Avoids new tools out of **embarrassment** with younger colleagues, not principle.
Practical fall-backs rely on her **family**: her mum and her partner.

steps.text: Learn the new ordering system with Marcos if Pennant buys one
Look for customer desk jobs at the council through the job centre
Ask Mum to mind the kids two afternoons a week
Move the phones to the cheapest plan and cancel holidays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and somebody should slow it down. I don't know who, the government, I suppose. I'd be quiet at work, because who do you complain to? It's like complaining about the weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I lose my job inside two years. Marcos keeps his a while, because a van needs a driver, but I know the bread company would love a self-driving one. We'd be one wage, a mortgage and two kids, and that doesn't add up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the council and the job centre first thing and ask what exists, because I don't know. I'd try to get hours at my sister's salon, even sweeping floors. And I'd ask the bank to move the mortgage to interest only for a while. I'd cut everything except food and school shoes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, and a bit numb. I'd feel like I'm standing on a platform when the train's coming and I can't decide where to stand. I'd go quiet at home and the kids would pick up on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the three extra years for hands-on work mean for your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means Marcos's job and my sister's salon are safe longer. Hands on, people-facing, not easy for a robot. So the family has a little place to stand while I sort myself out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Beatriz and Tiago?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say Mum's work is changing, and we'll be okay because we have each other. Beatriz is twelve and she'd ask hard questions. I'd answer them honestly, I think, but not the money ones.

say: I'd say it's too fast and somebody should **slow** it down.
I'd stay quiet at work, because there's no one to **complain** to.
think: I lose my job inside two years; my partner's bread van job lasts **longer**.
One wage, a mortgage and two kids **doesn't** add up.
do: Go to the council and the job centre first and ask what **help** exists.
Ask my sister for hours at her **salon**, even sweeping floors.
Ask the bank for an **interest-only** mortgage for a while, and cut everything but food and school shoes.
feel: **Alarmed** and numb, like standing on a platform not knowing where to stand.
S2.quote: I'd feel like I'm standing on a platform when the train's coming and I can't decide where to stand.
fieldNote: Shows **fatalism**: no one to blame, no plan, so she goes quiet and turns to family.
Sees her partner's and sister's hands-on, people-facing work as the **last footing**.
Would answer her daughter's hard questions honestly, except the **money** ones.

steps.text: Ask the council and job centre what help exists
Ask the bank to switch the mortgage to interest only for a while
Take sweeping and shop-floor hours at my sister's salon
Cut everything except food and school shoes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for the shop floor, but cold comfort for people in offices. I'd ask the owner what Pennant is doing about it. He'd probably say nothing yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In my head, I've got until my daughter nearly finishes school. That's something. But I know I tend to wait until the last minute, and the last minute with AI could be a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pick one thing and do it, which for me is a bookkeeping course at night, because my sister's salon needs one and so do other small places. I'd start putting away eighty a month, which is all we can do. And I'd practise the computer systems at work a little at a time, with Ivo showing me, because five years is long enough to stop being scared of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better than the two-year one. It's like having a deadline for a big job, I know I'll be stressed, but I can plan. Sometimes I'd forget about it for a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you tend to wait until the last minute. How would you stop yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the course fee on my credit card so I can't back out, and I'd tell my partner. If I tell him, I have to do it. I'm stubborn like that, so I use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your sister or Marcos to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marcos should look at a second certificate, like a forklift ticket, for his bread depot. Hands-on skills last longer. And my sister should start taking on apprentices before they're all gone.

say: I'd say five years is enough for the shop floor, but cold **comfort** for office workers.
I'd ask the owner what Pennant is doing about it, and he'd say **nothing** yet.
think: I've got until my daughter nearly finishes school, which is **something**.
I tend to wait until the last minute, and that could be a **cliff**.
do: Take a night **bookkeeping** course, since my sister's salon and other small places need one.
Put away **eighty** a month, which is all we can do.
Practise the work systems a little at a time with **Ivo** (my younger colleague).
feel: **Better** than at two years: a deadline I can plan around, though still stressful.
S3.quote: I tend to wait until the last minute, and the last minute with AI could be a cliff.
fieldNote: Extra time lets her **choose** one concrete thing, a bookkeeping course, over general worry.
Knows her habit of **delay** and plans to use her partner's accountability against it.
Thinks hands-on skills last longer and wants her family to have **them**.

steps.text: Take a night bookkeeping course and pay the fee by card
Put away eighty a month, which is all we can manage
Practise the work systems a little at a time with Ivo

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long enough that I'd say let the young ones sort it out. But I'd tell the kids to get a trade or a caring job. Not a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'll be fifty-three, and my kids will be nearly grown. I could be okay if I find something steady by then. But Pennant probably won't last ten years, with or without AI, so I can't count on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save more, aim for three months, and look at moving to a company that isn't in a shrinking trade. Hospitals and schools buy a lot of supplies. I'd try for a buyer job there, since it's the same skills, just a steadier customer. And I'd learn the computer side slowly, one thing a quarter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly a low worry, like having a sore tooth you ignore. I'd be calmer than with the short ones, but I'd still glance at the bank balance every Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a hospital job realistic for someone in your position?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a real option, a junior buyer is a junior buyer anywhere. They pay a bit more and don't go bust. The trouble is they hire slowly, and there are few of them near us, so I'd have to apply to everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Beatriz about her future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her to find something she's good at with her hands, or with people who are hurt or old. My mum was a care worker and she's never been out of work. A machine can't sit with a sick person.

say: I'd say ten years is long enough to let the **young** ones sort it out.
I'd tell my kids to get a **trade** or a caring job, not a screen.
think: I'll be fifty-three, and my kids nearly **grown**.
Pennant probably won't last ten years, with or without AI, so I can't **count** on it.
do: Apply for buyer jobs at hospitals and **schools**, a steadier customer for the same skills.
Learn one new computer **task** each quarter.
feel: A low **worry**, like a sore tooth I ignore; I'd still check the bank balance every Friday.
S4.quote: A machine can't sit with a sick person.
fieldNote: Ten years eases the **deadline** but not her fear for a shrinking firm.
Sees **hospitals and schools** as steadier buyers of the same skills she has.
Points her daughter toward **caring** work, drawing on her mum's long career.

steps.text: Save toward three months of expenses
Apply for junior buyer jobs at hospitals and schools
Learn one new computer task at work each quarter
Steer Beatriz toward caring or hands-on work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I wouldn't have time to learn anything, and we'd be down to one wage. What would help is time and someone showing me what to do, like a proper course with pay, not just a link. And a bit of help with the mortgage while I'm between things.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me aren't lazy about this. We just don't want to look stupid. If somebody sat with me for an hour and went slowly, I'd get it.

headlineQuote: We just don't want to look stupid. If somebody sat with me for an hour and went slowly, I'd get it.
portrait: Maya is a **43-year-old** junior buyer at a shrinking office supplies wholesaler, with a bread-van driver partner and two kids.
She is a pragmatic centrist, **fatalistic**, and blames no one in particular.
She never uses AI, delays change out of embarrassment, and would learn if **someone sat with her**.
She leans on family and small side jobs, and is **alarmed** when AGI arrives in 2028.
biggestWorry: The 2028 case, because she'd have no time to learn and the household would drop to **one wage**.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **training** with a real person showing her, plus mortgage help while she's between jobs.
